questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The mountains and beautiful nature - and how safe Switzerland is

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy - UZH sends out mails regularly and with clearly stated deadlines. They also answer emails quickly and are very helpful

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an intro meeting for exchange students with info about arriving in Switzerland and how UZH works

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I thought I would recieve accomodation through UZH since everyone I'd talked to who'd been there previously had been assigned accomodation but I ended up not getting one and having to find accomodation by myself. I found a half Swiss, half Danish family on Facebook who I lived with for two months (they were very, very nice and it was a great introduction to Swiss culture), until I moved to central Zürich into a student accomodation. I found this accomodation through
WOKO.ch
which is an organization affiliated with the universities in Zürich only for students under 28 - there was someone who was subletting their room and that's how I found it.
I know multiple people who did however end up getting accomodation through UZH - the standard place where everyone is put is Meierwiesenstrasse 62. I am so glad, I did not live there since it is 169 people sharing one industrial sized kitchen. I visited people living there multiple times and it looked very stressful and messy. If you are a person who can handle living with many other people, then you will be fine - but if you struggle in a slightly dirty and loud environment, then I'd seek out other accomodations.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
There are of course always scammers so be careful - if you can't find accomodation directly through
WOKO.ch
then try
wgzimmer.ch
- here you can search for flatshare with other students. I know multiple people who found great and cheap accomodation through here. But always be vigilant of course.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very easy - they have removed place limits on almost all courses, so even if you are late to book, you will most likely get a spot. And you can pick and choose courses until October 7th (for fall semester) which is nice since you can get to try out courses before you have to make your final decision.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The website is pretty complicated but they have videos on how to navigate it which helped greatly.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Apart from videoes they also answer emails quickly - the professors usually do as well

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted since there were no restrictions on number of students - very easy process!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I recommend signing up for more classes than just 30 ECTS and then trying them all out until registration closes so you are sure the professor is good and the course material is interesting. Many course descriptions were a bit lacking so really the only way to really know a course is to experience it. But remember to deregister of course!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It reeeeeeeeally depends. I took 5 courses since almost all courses at UZH Law are maximum 6 ECTS. I recommend you do not exceed 5 courses! Some of the courses were very complicated and others were extremely easy. It really depends. But in general the level is very high and there are a lot of expectations of the students. If you are looking to have a chill semester where you can slack off do NOT go to UZH. But if you are looking to learn a lot at a great institution then I would greatly recommend it.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was mostly seminar style teaching with the professor teaching from slides. All my classes were recorded which was a great help. There was also in many of my courses the oppourtunity to get extra credit by either doing student presentations or moot court or the like. I did not do any of this but I'm sure this could be enjoyable. Overall the professors were very nice and smart - but don't call them by their first name still.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Corruption and organized crime. 
Fintech, Blockchain and the Future of International Finance. 
Principles of corporate law.
International trade regulation.
Law and economics.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Corruption and organized crime is a very easy course with a nice professor - guaranteed pass.
Principles of corporate law had two great and skilled professors but requires a lot of work. I, however, learned a lot and had a great time.
International trade regulation was also a great course - the professor was really great and smart and classes were interesting and very relevant to todays climate.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It costs 55-70 CHF to register in Zürich, which is mandatory. If you move you have to pay this again.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Everything was more expensive - perhaps except croissants, they're the only cheap thing i Switzerland.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Free gym and gym classes and the like through the uni sports facility called ASVZ - download the app and register. It's great and everything is free.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to BQM on Polyterasse after classes. Introduce yourself to Swiss people in your courses. They're reserved but very nice! avoid paying for clubs or going to clubs on Saturday as it is more expensive than Friday (and Thursday is usually free).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go hiking every Sunday. Everything is closed anyway so Sunday is the perfect day - seriously! And try to go skiing as well!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The Swiss-Germans are very similar to Danish people - reserved but nice once you get to know them. But they are more polite in all ways.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just introduce yourself - I found getting to know Swiss students very easy. They're all great at English and very nice!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
None to be honest. I felt very at home quickly.
Maybe the fact that when Swiss people blow their nose, they do it veeery loudly, which is very annoying.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
How outdoorsy and inviting the people were. They also really love their country so they give great tips on what to see and what not to see. 
Everything is also very safe and proper - trains run on time and you don't feel unsafe walking alone at night as a girl. And trains and busses run all night on weekends which is very nice!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Make sure you have enough money!!!!! If you go to Zürich on a tight budget, you will not have much fun. It is absolutely one of the most expensive cities in the world, so don't go if you want to save money!
2. Try many different courses at UZH before choosing your final ones 
3. When UZH sends out an e-mail with all incoming students, contact all the Danish ones and make a group! We did this during our semester and we ended up going hiking together every Sunday and doing many other fun activites. You make great friends you can bring home and it ensures that you will not be lonely even for a second in a new country. Seriously!! This is a major hack!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Be aware that pretty much all written exams are written by hand on paper with pen and you have to print everything. Very old-school and your hand gets very tired from writing so much. 

But the main campus is so beautiful and everything was great!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Everything to be honest. But the hikes were next level.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Money. Switzerland is just crazy expensive - especially eating out.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
